newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: Slovak c.bank board changes put analysts on alert.
newsitem.headline: Slovak c.bank board changes put analysts on alert.

text.p: Changes to the governing board of the Slovak central bank (NBS) have put analysts on alert amid unresolved tension over monetary and fiscal policy.
The NBS declined to comment on any possible effect on its monetary policy of Tuesday's appointment by the government of former deputy finance minister Jozef Magula to its board.
Bankers have been closely watching for signs that government appointments to the eight-strong board might lead to a loss of central bank independence or a loosening of its tight monetary policy.

Government officials have repeatedly criticised NBS policy, which was further tightened late in 1996 after the government approved an expansionary fiscal deficit of 3.7 percent of GDP for this year, compared with a 0.4 percent surplus in 1996.

"The NBS's next steps should be closely watched with regard to Magula's past as defender of a certain (political) line, which may raise a suspicion he was appointed with a certain role," ING Barings analyst Martin Barto told Reuters.

Magula, one of most controversial Slovak government officials, said after he was replaced as deputy minister last week he had offered to resign because of his opposition to recent changes on the cappital market.
However, he is seen as a government loyalist and told Reuters his removal was the "result of an agreement".
The NBS said on Wednesday Magula would become a director of a soon to be established "Chamber of the Governor's advisers", but declined to specify its activities or powers.

By law, the central bank is independent but the government makes most appointments, based on NBS Governor Vladimir Masar's proposals, to its policy-making board. Parliament appoints the governor and his two deputies.

A bank spokesman said Masar would present a proposal next Tuesday to appoint NBS bank supervision department head Tibor Kasiak as another new board member and that the last vacant seat would be filled soon afterwards.

"One should not turn a blind eye to these changes, they are interesting, but what they mean for the NBS independence is still an open question...If Kasiak's proposal is ratified the balance may be maintained," a Western analyst said.
Some analysts said any major change to NBS policy could would require the replacement of either of the bank's two chief executive directors, who rank after Masar and his deputies.

"Unless one of the bank's chief executive directors is replaced, I think the changes are not crucial -- it seems impossible to change the NBS (policy) as it is at the present," said an analyst with a local bank.
The bank appeared to be sticking to its tight policy on Wednesday, offering to drain an unspecified volume of liquidity in a seven-day secrurities reverse repurchase tender.

Slovakia's key M2 money supply, buoyed by domestic lending, rose 15.7 percent for 1996, forcing the NBS to implement a series of tightening measures to curb consumption-oriented loan expansion and further cut inflation.
Imports have been sucked in and the current account swung to a deficit for the first 11 months of 1996 of $1.4 billion, compared with a $480.6 million surplus for the same period in 1995.
Western financial organisations have lauded Slovakia's tight monetary policy and have said fiscal policy should be framed to support it.
